title: Wallcovering Fire Ratings: British Standards and Commercial Specification
description: How reaction-to-fire classes such as B-s1,d0 are read, which standards and guidance apply in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and what makers' documents show for specific commercial wallcoverings.

scope.jurisdiction: England first (Approved Document B), with Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland set out separately. It is not legal advice, and it does not cover any country outside the UK.
scope.review: Makers and regulators can change their documents at any time. Each product row shows the date we last read its documents; ask the maker for its current declaration before relying on a row.
scope.notice: General specification guidance, not project-specific fire-safety approval. It has not been reviewed by a chartered fire engineer. Who confirms the class a wall or ceiling needs, and whether a proposed build-up achieves it, depends on the job: for building work, the designer or fire engineer with the building-control body. For redecorating a building in use that is not building work, the responsible person under fire-safety law confirms it, often with a fire risk assessor. Its main assessment and general fire-precaution duties do not apply inside a private home or, in Scotland and Northern Ireland, to the shared parts of a block of flats. A narrow duty to maintain facilities for firefighters still applies to those shared parts.

decoder.introduction: A European reaction-to-fire class has up to three parts: the main class (A1 to F), a smoke subclass (s1 to s3) and a flaming droplets subclass (d0 to d2). Read the notation exactly as the document prints it. For classes A2, B, C and D, a smoke or droplet subclass that is not printed is unknown, not assumed. Classes A1 and F carry no subclasses; class E carries no smoke subclass and is followed by d2 only if the filter paper ignited.

classes.label: highest
classes.meaning: The highest class. The product passes both the non-combustibility and the calorific-value tests. No smoke or droplet subclass is given.
classes.basis: BS EN ISO 1182 and BS EN ISO 1716.

classes.meaning: Passes one of the A1 tests to a less strict limit, and the single burning item test to the class B limits. Carries smoke and droplet subclasses.
classes.basis: BS EN ISO 1182 or BS EN ISO 1716, plus BS EN 13823: fire growth rate (FIGRA) up to 120 W/s, lateral flame spread short of the specimen edge, total heat release in 600 s up to 7.5 MJ.

classes.meaning: A limited contribution to fire growth in the single burning item test, and limited flame spread from a small flame.
classes.basis: BS EN 13823: FIGRA up to 120 W/s, lateral flame spread short of the specimen edge, total heat release in 600 s up to 7.5 MJ. BS EN ISO 11925-2: 30-second flame, flame spread no more than 150 mm within 60 seconds.

classes.meaning: As class B, with higher limits for fire growth and total heat release.
classes.basis: BS EN 13823: FIGRA up to 250 W/s, lateral flame spread short of the specimen edge, total heat release in 600 s up to 15 MJ. BS EN ISO 11925-2: 30-second flame, flame spread no more than 150 mm within 60 seconds.

classes.meaning: A higher fire-growth limit in the single burning item test and the same small-flame test as B and C.
classes.basis: BS EN 13823: FIGRA up to 750 W/s. BS EN ISO 11925-2: 30-second flame, flame spread no more than 150 mm within 60 seconds.

classes.meaning: Passes a shorter small-flame test only. May carry d2 if the filter paper ignites; no smoke subclass.
classes.basis: BS EN ISO 11925-2: 15-second flame, flame spread no more than 150 mm within 20 seconds.

classes.label: lowest
classes.meaning: Assigned when a product fails to attain class E. It is a class, not a blank: different from “no performance determined” and from an untested product.
classes.basis: BS EN ISO 11925-2: 15-second flame, flame spread more than 150 mm within 20 seconds (Delegated Regulation 2016/364, Table 1); England's Approved Document B, Appendix B, paragraph B6.

smoke.label: lowest smoke
smoke.meaning: The lowest smoke production category in the single burning item test.
smoke.basis: Smoke growth rate (SMOGRA) up to 30 m²/s² and total smoke production in 600 s up to 50 m².

smoke.meaning: More smoke allowed than s1, still within a limit.
smoke.basis: SMOGRA up to 180 m²/s² and total smoke production in 600 s up to 200 m².

smoke.label: no limit set
smoke.meaning: Neither s1 nor s2: no limit is set for smoke production.
smoke.basis: Not s1 or s2. Approved Document B: s3 means no limit is set.

droplets.label: none
droplets.meaning: No flaming droplets or particles in the single burning item test within 600 seconds.
No flaming droplets or particles that persist for longer than 10 seconds within 600 seconds.

droplets.label: no limit set
droplets.meaning: Neither d0 nor d1: no limit is set for flaming droplets. Also given when the filter paper ignites in the small-flame test.
droplets.basis: Not d0 or d1; or paper ignition in BS EN ISO 11925-2.

standards.title: Fire classification of construction products and building elements. Classification using data from reaction to fire tests

standards.title: Reaction to fire tests. Ignitability of products subjected to direct impingement of flame. Single-flame source test

notes: Note 1 to the table (on the circulation-space row): wallcoverings conforming to BS EN 15102, achieving at least class C-s3,d2 and bonded to a class A2-s3,d2 substrate, are also acceptable.

Paragraph 6.4: parts of walls in rooms may be of lower performance, but no worse than D-s3,d2, with the total lower-performance area less than half the room's floor area and no more than 20 m² (residential) or 60 m² (non-residential).

Paragraphs 6.2 to 6.6 define what counts as a wall and a ceiling; paragraph 6.12 points to further guidance for escape stairs, firefighting shafts and surfaces above fire-protecting suspended ceilings.

jurisdictions.name: Scotland
jurisdictions.document: Building standards technical handbooks: non-domestic (linings table below) and domestic
jurisdictions.edition: April 2026 handbooks (both published 9 March 2026), for building warrants submitted on or after 6 April 2026 and for building work that needs no warrant started on or after that date
jurisdictions.linings: Non-domestic handbook: Standard 2.5 and Table 2.4 give European classes by building group (residential care buildings and hospitals, shops, all other buildings) and by location (rooms up to and over 30 m², unprotected zones, and protected zones and fire-fighting shafts). Domestic handbook: protected zones A1, A2 or B; rooms, unprotected zones and protected enclosures no worse than C; small rooms and limited wall areas D (clause 2.5.1). In both, clause 2.5.1 defines wall and ceiling surfaces as the substrate or lining material, excluding decorative wallpaper and paints, and says multiple layers can increase flame spread and are not recommended when redecorating.
jurisdictions.nationalClasses: Not used for linings: reaction-to-fire classification uses European classes only (Annex 2.E, Table 2.20). The non-domestic handbook still accepts national BS 476 tests for fire resistance (Annex 2.D, clause 2.D.4, BS 476 Parts 20 to 24) and for roof coverings (Annex 2.F, BS 476-3). Where the non-domestic handbook gives a lining class without subclasses, s3,d2 is deemed included (Annex 2.E).

dates.label: April 2026 handbooks apply (by building warrant date, or start date for work that needs no warrant)

notes: Clause 2.5.1 of both handbooks excludes decorative wallpaper and paints from the classified surface but does not define them. Where the work needs a building warrant, agree with the verifier whether a given wallcovering is treated as decoration or as lining. Work that needs no warrant must still meet the building regulations, and the owner or client has the duty to comply. Both warn that multiple decorative layers can increase flame spread.

sources.title: The Building Regulations 2010, Schedule 1, Part B, and regulation 7
sources.establishes: The legal requirement for internal linings (requirement B2 in Schedule 1 to the Building Regulations 2010) and regulation 7 on materials.

sources.title: The Building Regulations 2010, regulation 3 (meaning of building work)
sources.establishes: An alteration is 'material' only if it affects a 'relevant requirement': Part A, B1, B3, B4, B5, Part M or Part T. B2 (internal linings) is not on the list, so redecorating on its own is not normally building work.
sources.limits: The text applies in England; Wales has its own amendments to the same regulations (the Welsh Volume 2, paragraph 0.18, gives the same list for Part B).

sources.title: Building Act 1984, sections 6 and 7
sources.establishes: The status of approved documents: approved under section 6, and under section 7 compliance or non-compliance may be relied on as tending to establish or negative liability.

sources.title: Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, articles 3, 8, 9 and 50
sources.establishes: Fire safety in buildings in use in England and Wales, other than inside private homes: the responsible person's duties to take general fire precautions and to keep a fire risk assessment under review, including after significant changes, extensions or conversions (article 9(3)).

sources.title: Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, article 2 (interpretation)
sources.establishes: 'Domestic premises' means premises occupied as a private dwelling, including appurtenances not used in common by the occupants of more than one dwelling; shared halls and stairs are therefore not domestic premises.

sources.title: Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, article 3 (meaning of "responsible person")
sources.establishes: The responsible person is the employer, for a workplace to any extent under its control; otherwise the person who controls the premises for a trade, business or other undertaking; or else the owner.

sources.title: Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, article 5 (duties under the Order)
sources.establishes: Anyone else with control of the premises to any extent shares the duties for matters within their control, including anyone whose contract or tenancy gives them an obligation for maintenance, repair or safety.

sources.title: Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, article 6 (application to premises)
sources.establishes: The Order does not apply to domestic premises (article 6(1)(a)); in a building with two or more sets of domestic premises it applies to the structure, external walls (including doors, windows and balconies) and common parts, and to the doors between the flats and the common parts (article 6(1A) and (1B), inserted by the Fire Safety Act 2021).

sources.title: Fire Safety Act 2021, section 1
sources.establishes: Inserts article 6(1A) and (1B) into the Fire Safety Order: in a building with two or more sets of domestic premises, the Order covers the structure, external walls (including doors, windows and balconies) and common parts, and the doors between the flats and the common parts. In force in Wales from 1 October 2021 and in England from 16 May 2022.
sources.limits: Applies to England and Wales only.

sources.issuer: Department for Communities and Local Government
sources.title: Fire safety risk assessment: sleeping accommodation
sources.reference: Guide published under article 50 of the Fire Safety Order
sources.establishes: Official fire risk assessment guidance for hotels and other sleeping accommodation in England and Wales. It discusses wall and ceiling linings and says care is needed with multi-layer decorative systems such as wallpapers and oil-based paints, in the older national class terms.
sources.limits: Written before the European classes replaced the national ones in English guidance; it says the European equivalent is acceptable.

sources.issuer: Department for Communities and Local Government
sources.title: Fire safety risk assessment: offices and shops
sources.reference: Guide published under article 50 of the Fire Safety Order
sources.establishes: The equivalent official guidance for offices and shops. It lists wall and ceiling linings by the older national classes and notes that additional finishes may harm a surface's fire performance.
sources.limits: Uses the older national class terms.

sources.title: The Building etc. (Amendment) (No. 2) (Wales) Regulations 2025

sources.title: The Building Safety (Description of Higher-Risk Building) (Design and Construction Phase) (Wales) Regulations 2023
sources.establishes: In Wales, a higher-risk building for design and construction is at least 18 m or seven storeys and contains at least one residential unit, a hospital with an overnight bed, a care home or a children's home (regulation 3); a building comprised entirely of a hotel is excluded (regulation 6).

sources.title: Fire (Scotland) Act 2005, section 78
sources.establishes: The Part 3 fire safety duties do not apply to domestic premises, which include a stair or passage used in common by the occupants of more than one dwelling; houses that must be licensed as houses in multiple occupation are not domestic premises, so the duties apply to them.

sources.title: Fire (Scotland) Act 2005, section 53 (duties of employers)
sources.establishes: Each employer must assess the workplace for fire risks and take fire-safety measures.

sources.title: Fire (Scotland) Act 2005, section 54 (duties in relation to relevant premises)
sources.establishes: Anyone with control of relevant premises to any extent must assess fire risks and take fire-safety measures to that extent; in some cases the owner; and anyone whose contract or tenancy gives them an obligation for maintenance, repair or fire safety.

sources.title: Fire Safety (Scotland) Regulations 2006, regulation 24
sources.establishes: Applies the duty to maintain measures provided for the protection of firefighters (regulation 23) to the common areas of private dwellings, for persons with control of those areas.

sources.title: Building (Scotland) Regulations 2004, regulation 5 (building warrant exemptions)
sources.establishes: Work of a kind listed in schedule 3 must meet the standards but does not need a building warrant, subject to the exceptions and conditions.

sources.title: Building (Scotland) Regulations 2004, schedule 3 (work not requiring a warrant)
sources.establishes: Replacing flooring, lining, covering or rendering, in whole or in part, by material of the same general type, internally or externally, needs no building warrant, on condition that the work is to a standard no worse than at present.

checklists.title: Before ordering
checklists.intro: Collect these for each wallcovering and each area it is going into.
items: The exact product: maker, collection, product reference, colourway or design, and whether it is a stock or digitally printed version.
The construction as supplied: face material, backing, weight and any finish or protective coating.

The requirement for each area: the class set for it, and whether the area is a room, a small room or a circulation space. For building work, the project's fire strategy, designer or building-control body sets the class. For a building in use where the job is not building work, the responsible person sets it, through the fire risk assessment.
The evidence: the current declaration of performance and, where available, the classification report for that product, with their references and dates.
The tested build-up: the substrate, adhesive and any primer or lining named in the classification document, and the field of application it allows.
The proposed build-up on site: the actual wall, any existing finishes, the lining, primer and adhesive to be used, and any coating to be added.

Any difference between the two, with the maker's written position and any test or assessment report relied on. Record who accepted it: for building work, the designer, fire engineer or building-control body; where the job is not building work, the responsible person.
The maker's installation instructions for that product, current at the time of ordering.

checklists.title: At handover
checklists.intro: Keep a record of what was actually installed, so it can be checked later.
items: A room-by-room or area-by-area schedule of the products installed: reference, colourway and batch number.
Copies of the declaration of performance, classification evidence and installation instructions relied on, with their dates.
The adhesive, primer and lining actually used, with batch numbers where practical, and the substrate each area was hung on.
Any accepted variation from the documented build-up, with the maker's written position, any test or assessment report relied on, and who accepted it.
Photographs of the prepared substrate before hanging, where the project calls for them.
Care and cleaning instructions, including any limit on later coatings or overpainting that would change the build-up.
Spare material from the same batch, labelled, for future repairs.

faq.q: What does B-s1,d0 mean on a wallcovering?
faq.a: It is a European reaction-to-fire classification under BS EN 13501-1: class B for the main fire behaviour, s1 for the lowest smoke production category and d0 for no flaming droplets or particles in the test. It applies to the product as tested, in the build-up the classification document describes.

faq.q: Is B-s2,d0 good enough for a hotel corridor?
faq.a: That depends on the requirement set for that corridor. In England, Approved Document B Volume 2 (buildings other than dwellings) gives a minimum of B-s3,d2 for circulation spaces in its Table 6.1, which B-s2,d0 meets, but a project's fire strategy can set a higher requirement, and the product must be installed in the build-up its classification covers. The designer, fire engineer or building-control body decides, or, for a building in use where the job is not building work, the responsible person through the fire risk assessment.

faq.q: A data sheet says only 'Euroclass B'. Is that the same as B-s1,d0?
faq.a: No. 'Euroclass B' without smoke and droplet subclasses tells you the main class only. Treat the subclasses as unknown and ask the maker for the declaration of performance or classification report, which will state them.

faq.q: Is Class 0 the same as a Euroclass?
faq.a: No. Class 0 is an old British national classification: a material of limited combustibility throughout, or a BS 476 Part 7 Class 1 material that also meets BS 476 Part 6 fire propagation limits. It was defined in earlier editions of England's Approved Document B and is still printed in the Welsh and Northern Irish guidance. It is not the result of any single test, and there is no automatic conversion between Class 0 and a European class. England's guidance stopped offering national reaction-to-fire classes as an alternative from 2 March 2025, subject to transitional arrangements.

faq.q: Does a fire-rated wallcovering make a wall fire resistant?
faq.a: No. A wallcovering's class describes its reaction to fire: how it contributes to the early growth of a fire. Fire resistance, expressed in minutes, belongs to walls, floors and doors as building elements, and a wallcovering does not provide it.

faq.q: Can a classified wallcovering be hung over old wallpaper or lining paper?
faq.a: Only if the maker's documents cover it, or a test or assessment report covers that build-up. The designer, fire engineer or building-control body then has to accept it, or, for a building in use where the job is not building work, the responsible person. Hanging over an existing wallcovering adds an untested layer, and makers' instructions generally ask for old wallcoverings to be removed. Lining paper, a different adhesive or a later coating are also changes to the build-up.

faq.q: Does Mr Wallcover certify the fire rating of what it installs?
faq.a: No. Classification comes from testing and classification of the product in a stated build-up, and the manufacturer declares the performance. We install the specified product to the maker's instructions and record what was installed. The designer, fire engineer or building-control body accepts the evidence, or, for a building in use where the job is not building work, the responsible person through the fire risk assessment.

faq.q: Do these rules apply in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland?
faq.a: Wales applies the Building Regulations 2010 as amended for Wales, with its own Approved Document B. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own building regulations, with the Technical Handbooks and Technical Booklet E as guidance. They use the same European classes, but their tables, terms and amendment dates differ, so check the guidance for where the building is.
